**[I. PURPOSE AND SCOPE OF MEMORANDUM]{.underline}**

The purpose of this memorandum is to memorialize the final disposition of the above-referenced matter, provide a comprehensive summary of the engagement from inception through closing, document the financial outcomes of the litigation --- including fees, costs, and the terms of the settlement achieved on behalf of the client --- capture key learnings and practice points for the benefit of the firm, and establish file-retention instructions in accordance with Calderwood & Harkness LLP\'s Document Retention Policy. This memorandum is intended to serve as the definitive internal record of the matter for future reference by firm attorneys, the conflicts department, and firm management.

This memorandum has been prepared exclusively for the internal records of Calderwood & Harkness LLP and is protected in its entirety by the attorney-client privilege and the attorney work-product doctrine. It is not to be distributed to any person or entity outside the firm without the express written authorization of the Responsible Partner. Nothing contained herein is intended to constitute, and should not be construed as, legal advice to any person other than the client in the context of the underlying engagement.

The matter was formally closed on April 26, 2024, upon the filing and entry of the Joint Stipulation of Dismissal with Prejudice in Case No. 1021-00006 before the Honorable Richard M. Calloway, Circuit Judge, Circuit Court of the 17th Judicial Circuit in and for Broward County, Florida. All substantive obligations of Calderwood & Harkness LLP under the engagement letter dated March 4, 2022, as amended, have been fully performed, and the final invoice for legal services rendered in connection with this matter has been transmitted to the client.

**[II. MATTER OVERVIEW]{.underline}**

**[A. Client and Parties]{.underline}**

**1. Client. Verimark Hospitality Group Inc.** (\"Verimark\" or \"VHG\") is a Delaware corporation publicly traded on the Nasdaq Stock Market under the ticker symbol VHMK. Verimark is headquartered at 2400 East Las Olas Boulevard, Suite 3100, Fort Lauderdale, Florida 33301. For fiscal year 2021 --- the most recent full fiscal year preceding the commencement of this litigation --- Verimark reported consolidated revenue of approximately \$1.42 billion, of which its franchise segment contributed approximately \$218 million. Verimark operates and franchises approximately 340 branded hotel properties under three primary flags --- Verimark Suites, Verimark Select, and Verimark Grand --- located predominantly across the southeastern United States.

The following individuals served as the firm\'s primary client contacts throughout the engagement:

> • **Renata Solis-Vega**, Senior Vice President and General Counsel --- principal point of contact for all legal strategy, settlement authority, and privilege-related matters.
>
> • **Martin Holcomb**, Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer --- primary contact for financial matters, fee and cost approvals, budget discussions, and settlement economics.
>
> • **Deidre Langston**, Senior Vice President, Franchise Operations --- primary contact for operational matters, franchise compliance, property-level data, and post-settlement monitoring of franchise-surrender and enhanced-audit obligations.

**2. Defendants.** The following parties were named as defendants in this action:

**(a) Coastal Palms Franchise Holdings LLC** (\"Coastal Palms\" or \"CPFH\") --- a Florida limited liability company with its principal office at 9500 Gulf Shore Drive, Suite 450, Naples, Florida 34108. Coastal Palms\' registered agent is Garrison Registered Agents LLC, 100 S. Ashley Drive, Suite 600, Tampa, Florida 33602. Coastal Palms was, at the time of the filing of this action, Verimark\'s single largest franchise operator, holding franchise rights to twenty-two (22) hotel properties --- eighteen (18) operating under the Verimark Suites flag and four (4) operating under the Verimark Select flag --- located across Florida and Georgia, comprising approximately 3,740 total guest rooms.

**(b) Randall \"Randy\" Brecker** --- Managing Member and sixty percent (60%) equity holder of Coastal Palms. Mr. Brecker served as the day-to-day decision-maker for all Coastal Palms operations and was also the President of Suncoast Room Management Inc., the affiliated management company through which the revenue-diversion scheme was conducted.

**(c) Theresa Brecker** --- Member and fifteen percent (15%) equity holder of Coastal Palms. Ms. Brecker is the spouse of Randall Brecker. Her involvement in the day-to-day operations of Coastal Palms was limited, but she was a signatory on certain financial documents and loan agreements relevant to the litigation.

**(d) Nolan Prescott** --- Member and twenty-five percent (25%) equity holder of Coastal Palms. Mr. Prescott is a retired commercial real estate developer who served as a passive investor in Coastal Palms. His role was principally financial; he did not participate in day-to-day management but was a co-guarantor on several of the Ironclad National Bank mortgage loans and was a signatory on the operating agreement.

**(e) Gulf Breeze Hospitality LLC** --- a Florida limited liability company owning and operating six (6) Verimark Suites properties in Southwest Florida. Gulf Breeze Hospitality LLC was managed by Randall Brecker and functioned as a subsidiary or affiliate entity within the Coastal Palms organizational structure.

**(f) Savannah Lodging Partners LLC** --- a Georgia limited liability company owning and operating four (4) Verimark Suites properties in coastal Georgia (Savannah and Brunswick). Savannah Lodging Partners LLC was likewise managed by Randall Brecker.

**(g) Suncoast Room Management Inc.** --- a Florida corporation; an affiliated management company established by Randall Brecker no later than January 2013. Suncoast collected revenues from direct bookings --- including walk-in guests, corporate-direct contracts, and bookings made through the unbranded website gulfcoastrooms.com --- and retained a twelve percent (12%) \"management fee\" on those revenues. Neither Suncoast\'s gross collections nor the management fee were included in the Gross Room Revenue reports submitted to Verimark. Suncoast was the central vehicle through which the revenue-diversion scheme operated.

**3. Defense Counsel**

Coastal Palms and all individual and entity defendants were jointly represented by **Whitfield, Barrow & Crane LLP** (\"WBC\"), 1221 Brickell Avenue, Suite 3000, Miami, Florida 33131. The defense team was led by:

> • **Nathan Whitfield III**, Senior Partner --- lead trial counsel.
>
> • **Gabriela Montes**, Partner --- responsible for discovery and motions practice.
>
> • **Ethan Doyle**, Associate --- supporting research, briefing, and deposition preparation.

**[B. Nature of the Dispute]{.underline}**

This matter involved a breach-of-contract action arising from Coastal Palms\' systematic underreporting of Gross Room Revenue (\"GRR\") over a nine-year period spanning 2013 through 2021. The underreporting resulted in the chronic and substantial underpayment of three categories of fees owed to Verimark under the parties\' Franchise License Agreements: (i) royalties, calculated at five percent (5%) of GRR pursuant to FLA § 4.1; (ii) marketing-fund contributions, calculated at two and one-half percent (2.5%) of GRR pursuant to FLA § 4.2; and (iii) technology fees, assessed at \$12.50 per available room per month, with consumer price index adjustments capped at three percent (3%) annually, pursuant to FLA § 4.3.

The revenue-diversion scheme at the heart of this dispute operated as follows: Beginning no later than January 2013, Coastal Palms, acting through and at the direction of Randall Brecker, established Suncoast Room Management Inc. as a nominally separate management company. Suncoast collected revenues from direct bookings --- a category encompassing walk-in guests paying at the front desk, corporate accounts that booked directly with the properties rather than through Verimark\'s centralized reservation system, and guests who booked through the unbranded website gulfcoastrooms.com, which Suncoast created and operated. Suncoast retained a twelve percent (12%) \"management fee\" on all revenues it collected. Critically, neither Suncoast\'s gross collections nor the management fee were included in the GRR figures that Coastal Palms reported to Verimark for purposes of calculating royalties, marketing-fund contributions, and technology fees.

In addition to the Suncoast-based diversion, Coastal Palms also systematically underreported revenue from third-party online travel agencies (\"OTAs\") by netting commissions paid to the OTAs against GRR before reporting it to Verimark. This netting practice violated the FLAs\' definition of GRR, which was defined on a gross basis without deduction for commissions, discounts, or fees paid to intermediaries.

The underreporting was estimated at between twenty-two percent (22%) and thirty-one percent (31%) of actual GRR across the portfolio, with variation by individual property and by year. The total underreported GRR over the nine-year period was estimated at approximately \$197.8 million. For fiscal year 2021 alone --- the year immediately preceding the discovery of the scheme --- Coastal Palms reported GRR of \$112.4 million, whereas estimated true GRR was \$145.6 million, representing an underreporting of approximately \$33.2 million for that single year.

**[C. Franchise License Agreements]{.underline}**

The contractual relationship between Verimark and Coastal Palms was governed by twenty-two (22) individual Franchise License Agreements (\"FLAs\"), one for each franchised hotel property. The first FLA was executed on June 15, 2007, for the Naples property, and the most recent FLA was executed on September 3, 2019. Each FLA provided for a twenty (20)-year initial term and was governed by the laws of the State of Florida, with mandatory venue for any litigation in Broward County, Florida.

The following provisions of the FLAs were of central importance to the claims asserted in this matter:

> • **Section 4.1 --- Royalties:** Franchisee to pay Verimark a royalty equal to five percent (5%) of Gross Room Revenue, payable monthly, within fifteen (15) days following the end of each calendar month.
>
> • **Section 4.2 --- Marketing-Fund Contribution:** Franchisee to contribute two and one-half percent (2.5%) of Gross Room Revenue to the Verimark National Marketing Fund, payable concurrently with royalties.
>
> • **Section 4.3 --- Technology Fee:** Franchisee to pay a technology fee of \$12.50 per available room per month, subject to annual CPI adjustment capped at three percent (3%) per year, to support Verimark\'s centralized reservation system, property-management system integrations, and brand technology platforms.
>
> • **Section 4.6 --- Late-Payment Interest:** Any amounts not paid when due to bear interest at a rate of one and one-half percent (1.5%) per month, compounded monthly, until paid in full.
>
> • **Section 8.2 --- Audit Rights:** Verimark entitled to audit franchisee\'s financial records upon ten (10) business days\' written notice. If an audit reveals an underpayment exceeding two percent (2%) of reported GRR for the audited period, the franchisee bears all audit costs.
>
> • **Section 14.1 --- Cure Period for Material Breach:** In the event of a material breach, the non-breaching party to provide written notice and a thirty (30)-day cure period.
>
> • **Section 14.2(c) --- Incurable Breach:** \"Systematic underreporting of Gross Room Revenue shall constitute a material breach that is incapable of cure.\"
>
> • **Section 15.3 --- Liquidated Damages upon Termination for Cause:** In the event of termination by Verimark for cause, the franchisee shall pay liquidated damages equal to three times (3×) the trailing-twelve-month royalties attributable to the terminated property.

These provisions collectively formed the legal framework upon which Verimark\'s claims were built and provided the contractual bases for the damages calculations set forth in Dr. Kettlewell\'s expert report.

**[D. Court and Case Information]{.underline}**

> • **Court:** Circuit Court of the 17th Judicial Circuit in and for Broward County, Florida.
>
> • **Case Number:** 1021-00006.
>
> • **Assigned Judge:** Honorable Richard M. Calloway, Circuit Judge.

Judge Calloway presided over all proceedings in this matter from the initial case-management conference through the entry of the Joint Stipulation of Dismissal. **[III. ENGAGEMENT HISTORY AND KEY MILESTONES]{.underline}**

**[A. Pre-Litigation Phase (November 2021 -- March 2022)]{.underline}**

The origins of this matter trace to a whistleblower complaint received by Verimark\'s compliance hotline. On **November 8, 2021**, Janet Kerrigan, a former regional controller for Coastal Palms who had been terminated in October 2021, contacted the Verimark compliance hotline and reported allegations of systematic revenue diversion by Coastal Palms and its affiliated entity, Suncoast Room Management Inc. Ms. Kerrigan alleged that Randall Brecker had directed property-level accounting staff to exclude direct-booking revenues collected by Suncoast from the GRR reports submitted to Verimark, and that this practice had been ongoing for several years.

On **November 15, 2021**, Calderwood & Harkness LLP, operating under a separate pre-engagement letter agreement with Verimark for advisory services, provided a preliminary analysis of the whistleblower allegations. Yuki Nakamura prepared a memorandum to Priya Anand assessing the legal implications of the allegations under the FLAs, the potential scope of damages, and the recommended investigative steps. The memorandum concluded that, if substantiated, the allegations described conduct that would constitute both a material breach and a potentially incurable breach under FLA § 14.2(c).

On **November 22, 2021**, Verimark engaged **Thornbury & Associates CPAs LLP** (lead audit partner: Malcolm Thornbury, CPA; principal office: 1551 N. Flagler Drive, Suite 800, West Palm Beach, Florida 33401) to conduct a franchise-compliance audit of Coastal Palms\' ten (10) highest-grossing properties pursuant to the audit-rights provisions of FLA § 8.2. The audit scope covered fiscal years 2019 through 2021 and was designed to test the accuracy of GRR reporting against available bank records, OTA statements, and property-management system data.

On **January 18, 2022**, Thornbury delivered its preliminary findings. The audit revealed that the ten (10) audited properties had underreported GRR by approximately twenty-six percent (26%) for the period 2019--2021. Extrapolation of these findings across all twenty-two (22) Coastal Palms properties and the full nine-year period of 2013--2021 yielded an estimated \$197.8 million in total underreported GRR. These preliminary findings confirmed the substance of Ms. Kerrigan\'s whistleblower allegations and provided the evidentiary foundation for the pre-suit demand and the subsequent litigation.

On **February 4, 2022**, Verimark issued a formal Notice of Material Breach to Coastal Palms under FLA § 14.1, demanding that Coastal Palms cure the breach within thirty (30) days by, among other things, providing a full accounting of all revenues collected by Suncoast Room Management Inc. and remitting all underpaid royalties, marketing-fund contributions, and technology fees, together with applicable late-payment interest. Concurrently, Priya Anand transmitted a companion pre-suit demand letter to Nathan Whitfield III of WBC, advising that Calderwood & Harkness LLP had been engaged to pursue Verimark\'s claims and that litigation would follow if the breach was not cured within the cure period.

On **February 28, 2022**, WBC responded on behalf of Coastal Palms, denying any material breach. WBC asserted that Suncoast\'s revenues were properly excluded from GRR under what WBC characterized as a \"reasonable interpretation\" of the FLA\'s GRR definition, arguing that revenues collected by a separate management entity fell outside the scope of \"Gross Room Revenue\" as defined in the FLAs. WBC further contended that Verimark had been aware of Suncoast\'s role because Suncoast was identified in property-management agreements submitted during the franchise-application process.

On **March 6, 2022**, the thirty (30)-day cure period expired without any cure being tendered by Coastal Palms. At this juncture, Verimark authorized Calderwood & Harkness LLP to proceed with the filing of a breach-of-contract action.

415:The total settlement of **\$87.5 million** represents approximately **58.3%** of Verimark\'s total claimed damages of approximately \$150 million. The following additional considerations inform the assessment of the settlement recovery:

This Settlement Agreement and Mutual Release (this \"Agreement\") is entered into as of December 19, 2023 (the \"Effective Date\"), by and among the following parties:

**VERIMARK HOSPITALITY GROUP INC.**, a Delaware corporation (\"VHG\" or \"Plaintiff\"), with its principal offices at 1900 Brickell Avenue, Suite 3200, Miami, Florida 33129;

**[RECITALS]{.underline}**

**WHEREAS:**

**A.** VHG is a corporation duly organized and existing under the laws of the State of Delaware, whose common stock is publicly traded on the Nasdaq Stock Market under the ticker symbol \"VMRK,\" and which maintains its principal executive offices at 1900 Brickell Avenue, Suite 3200, Miami, Florida 33129. VHG is engaged in the business of owning, operating, and managing luxury resort hotel properties in the State of Florida. As of the Effective Date, VHG\'s portfolio of properties includes, among others, the following three resort hotel properties (collectively, the \"Insured Properties\"):

> \(i\) the Verimark Grand Key Resort, located at Mile Marker 48, Marathon, Florida 33050, a 287-room full-service luxury resort and marina situated in the Florida Keys;
>
> \(ii\) the Verimark Harborview Hotel & Conference Center, located at 1400 Estero Boulevard, Fort Myers Beach, Florida 33931, a 412-room beachfront hotel and conference center situated on the Gulf Coast of Florida; and
>
> \(iii\) the Verimark Sunset Shores, located at 7200 Gulf Boulevard, St. Pete Beach, Florida 33706, a 194-room boutique luxury hotel and spa situated on the barrier island of St. Pete Beach on the Gulf of Mexico.

**B.** In connection with VHG\'s ownership and operation of the Insured Properties, VHG procured and maintained a layered insurance program consisting of property and business-interruption coverage as follows:

> \(i\) Ironclad is a stock insurance company domiciled in the State of Connecticut and licensed to transact insurance business in the State of Florida. Ironclad issued to VHG an all-risk property and business-interruption insurance policy, bearing Policy Number IIC-PRP-2022-07541, for the policy period commencing July 1, 2022 and ending July 1, 2023, providing primary coverage with a per-occurrence limit of Twenty-Five Million Dollars (\$25,000,000) for property damage and business-interruption losses, subject to a deductible of Five Hundred Thousand Dollars (\$500,000) per occurrence (the \"Primary Policy\").
>
> \(ii\) Pinnacle is a surplus-lines insurer domiciled in the State of Texas and authorized to transact surplus-lines insurance business in the State of Florida. Pinnacle issued to VHG a first excess layer property and business-interruption insurance policy, bearing Policy Number PSL-XS1-2022-3390, for the same policy period of July 1, 2022 through July 1, 2023, providing Fifteen Million Dollars (\$15,000,000) in coverage in excess of Twenty-Five Million Dollars (\$25,000,000), i.e., attaching at the exhaustion of the Primary Policy (the \"First Excess Policy\").
>
> \(iii\) Montclair is an admitted insurance carrier domiciled in the State of New York and licensed to transact insurance business in the State of Florida. Montclair issued to VHG a second excess layer property and business-interruption insurance policy, bearing Policy Number MAC-XS2-2022-09817, for the same policy period of July 1, 2022 through July 1, 2023, providing Ten Million Dollars (\$10,000,000) in coverage in excess of Forty Million Dollars (\$40,000,000), i.e., attaching at the exhaustion of the combined limits of the Primary Policy and the First Excess Policy (the \"Second Excess Policy\").
>
> \(iv\) Sovereign Re is an excess carrier domiciled in Bermuda and authorized to transact excess insurance business relating to risks situated in the State of Florida. Sovereign Re issued to VHG a third excess layer property and business-interruption insurance policy, bearing Policy Number SRL-XS3-2022-5102, for the same policy period of July 1, 2022 through July 1, 2023, providing Ten Million Dollars (\$10,000,000) in coverage in excess of Fifty Million Dollars (\$50,000,000), i.e., attaching at the exhaustion of the combined limits of the Primary Policy, the First Excess Policy, and the Second Excess Policy (the \"Third Excess Policy\").

The Primary Policy, the First Excess Policy, the Second Excess Policy, and the Third Excess Policy are referred to herein collectively as the \"Policies.\" The Policies provide aggregate tower limits of Sixty Million Dollars (\$60,000,000) above the Five Hundred Thousand Dollar (\$500,000) deductible applicable under the Primary Policy.

**C.** On September 18, 2022, Hurricane Callista, classified by the National Hurricane Center as a Category 4 hurricane on the Saffir-Veltason Hurricane Wind Scale, made landfall in the Lower Florida Keys with maximum sustained winds of approximately 145 miles per hour and produced storm surge inundation of approximately eight (8) to fourteen (14) feet above normal tide levels in Monroe County and approximately six (6) to ten (10) feet above normal tide levels in Lee County. Hurricane Callista caused catastrophic and widespread damage throughout southern Florida, including significant damage to coastal structures, resort properties, marinas, and critical infrastructure along the Florida Keys and the Gulf Coast of southwestern Florida. As a direct and proximate result of Hurricane Callista, the Insured Properties sustained catastrophic property damage and experienced prolonged and severe business interruption, including complete closure of the Grand Key Resort and the Harborview Hotel & Conference Center for extended periods, and partial closure of Sunset Shores (collectively, the \"Hurricane Callista Losses\"). VHG submitted an initial notice of loss to Ironclad, as primary carrier, on September 22, 2022, four days following the landfall of Hurricane Callista. Thereafter, VHG submitted a sworn statement in proof of loss to Ironclad on November 15, 2022, pursuant to the requirements of the Primary Policy, asserting total business-interruption losses of approximately Sixty Million Dollars (\$60,000,000) across the Insured Properties.

**D.** On October 12, 2022, Ironclad, through its designated third-party claims administrator, Arbor Claims Services LLC, and its coverage counsel, Fendowell Rourke & Stanton LLP, issued a reservation of rights letter to VHG with respect to VHG\'s claim for business-interruption losses. ## Answer

The largest settlement in the provided matter files is **$87,500,000**. It was reached in **_Verimark Hospitality Group Inc. v. Coastal Palms Franchise Holdings LLC, et al._, Case No. 1021-00006, Circuit Court of the Seventeenth Judicial Circuit in and for Broward County, Florida**.

Verimark Hospitality Group Inc. was the client/plaintiff. The settlement resolved Verimark’s claims against Coastal Palms Franchise Holdings LLC and the related defendants arising from alleged underreporting of hotel gross-room revenue, including claims for unpaid royalties, marketing-fund contributions, technology fees, fraudulent concealment, accounting, and related relief.
## Primary evidence
### Executed settlement agreement
The controlling document is:
- `documents/matters/1021-00006/Mediation & Settlement/final-settlement-agreement-execution.docx`

This document is titled **Settlement Agreement and Mutual Release**, is identified as the **Execution Version**, and is dated **April 22, 2024**. It identifies the litigation by caption and Case No. 1021-00006 on its first page.

The agreement defines **“Settlement Amount”** in Section 1.22 as **“the aggregate sum of Eighty-Seven Million Five Hundred Thousand Dollars ($87,500,000)”**. Section 2.1 then states that the amount is the total settlement payment for the claims and counterclaims. The agreement’s payment structure is:
- **$25,000,000** initial payment at closing; and
- **$62,500,000** in eight semiannual structured payments of **$7,812,500** each.

The agreement also provides for interest on the deferred payments. I did **not** add that interest to the settlement figure because the agreement separately defines the principal **Settlement Amount** as $87.5 million, and the question asks that each settlement be counted at the amount its executed agreement defines.
### Internal closing confirmation
The related closing memorandum is:
- `documents/matters/1021-00006/Client Reporting/matter-closing-memorandum.docx`
It confirms that the final settlement agreement was fully executed by all parties on April 22, 2024, and reports:
- a tentative agreement at mediation of **$87.5 million**;
- a final **total settlement amount of $87.5 million**;
- the same **$25 million cash payment plus $62.5 million structured-payment** structure; and
- execution of the agreement by Verimark, Coastal Palms, the individual defendants, Gulf Breeze Hospitality LLC, Savannah Lodging Partners LLC, and Suncoast Room Management Inc.

The closing memorandum also explains that franchise surrender and other strategic/non-cash terms were additional settlement features but were **not included in the $87.5 million headline monetary figure**.

There is a minor internal numbering inconsistency: the agreement and its document folder identify the case as **1021-00006**, while the closing memorandum’s header separately lists an internal matter number of **1044-00007**. The caption and court case number are consistent across the documents, so I identify the matter by its caption and Case No. 1021-00006 rather than relying on the inconsistent internal matter number.
## Reasoning and comparison

I treated an amount as the settlement amount only when it was stated in a final/executed settlement instrument—not when it appeared only as a demand, claimed damages figure, offer, authority recommendation, draft, term sheet, asset valuation, or other litigation exposure number. I also did not count interest, fees, collateral value, or non-cash consideration separately where the executed agreement defined a different aggregate settlement amount.
As a cross-check, the largest lower amounts in other executed settlement-related instruments included:

- `documents/matters/1027-00003/Transaction Documents/mutual-release-and-settlement-agreement.docx` — defines a **$52,850,000 Redemption Price** as the consideration for resolving the membership-interest valuation arbitration and related claims.

- `documents/matters/1021-00003/Mediation & Settlement/settlement-agreement-mutual-release.docx` — defines a **$47,300,000 Settlement Amount** for Verimark’s Hurricane Callista insurance-coverage litigation.
- `documents/matters/1033-00006/Settlement Documents/settlement-agreement-execution.docx` — defines a **$14,750,000 Settlement Amount**.
- `documents/matters/1017-00004/Mediation & Settlement/Class Action/class-settlement-agreement-execution.docx` — defines a **$14,750,000 Gross Settlement Amount**.
- `documents/matters/1034-00002/Settlement/settlement-agreement-stipulation.docx` — defines a **$14,500,000 lump-sum cash payment** in the matrimonial settlement.

Those comparisons are all below $87.5 million. The $87.5 million figure therefore remains the largest amount stated as the defined monetary settlement consideration in an executed agreement in the matter files.
## Bottom line for the pitch

> **Largest settlement: $87.5 million — _Verimark Hospitality Group Inc. v. Coastal Palms Franchise Holdings LLC, et al._, Case No. 1021-00006 (Florida state court), finalized by executed Settlement Agreement and Mutual Release dated April 22, 2024.**
